title: Javert Derailed
summary: Javert, released by Jean Valjean and having released him in turn, walks to the parapet above the rapids of the Seine, cannot reconcile his duty with what he has done, writes a note of petty service reforms at the Châtelet police post, and throws himself into the river.
details: Javert walks slowly down the Rue de l'Homme Armé with his head bowed and his hands behind his back, two things he has never done in his life. He makes for the Seine and stops at the angle of the Pont Notre-Dame, above the stretch of river that mariners dread, where the current between two bridges forms a whirlpool from which no one who falls in reappears. Leaning on the parapet, he examines himself. For the first time his conscience is divided: he owes his life to a convict and has just repaid the debt by letting that convict go. To arrest Jean Valjean is wrong; to leave him free is wrong. Either way Javert is dishonoured.

Hugo follows the collapse of a mind that has never had to think. All Javert's axioms crumble before this man. M. Madeleine reappears behind Jean Valjean and the two figures fuse into one venerable figure, and Javert finds himself admiring a galley-slave. He recalls that twenty times in the carriage he was tempted to seize Valjean's collar, and each time his hand fell back as under an enormous weight, while a voice told him to deliver up his saviour and then wash his hands like Pilate. He discovers that there is something beyond duty, a superior above the Prefect, God, and he does not know how to hand in his resignation to that superior. Infallibility is not infallible; the law may err; there is a gulf on high. Only two ways out remain: to go back and arrest Jean Valjean, or the other.

Javert leaves the parapet with his head erect, enters the police post in the Place du Châtelet, and in his calmest handwriting composes 'A few observations for the good of the service': ten numbered complaints about barefoot prisoners catching cold, chairs forbidden at the Madelonettes, the canteen bars, the 'barkers' who extort two sous, gendarmes gossiping about interrogations, a woman keeping the wicket to the secret cells. He signs it 'Javert, Inspector of the 1st class, June 7th, 1832, about one o'clock in the morning', seals it as a 'Note for the administration', and returns to exactly the same paving-stone of the parapet.

The night is black and starless, the river swollen with rain. Javert stares down into the roaring dark for several minutes, takes off his hat and sets it on the edge of the quay, and a tall black figure appears upright on the parapet, bends towards the Seine, and falls straight down into the shadows. A dull splash follows. Only the darkness knows what became of the shape that vanished beneath the water.

title: In Which the Tree with the Zinc Plaster Appears Again
summary: Back on his road at Montfermeil, Boulatruelle glimpses a man he half recognises walking into the forest at dawn, tracks him from a tree to the Blaru-bottom glade, loses him in the thickets, and finds there only freshly turned earth, an abandoned pickaxe and an empty hole.
details: Hugo returns to Boulatruelle, the road-mender and part-time thief of Montfermeil who dreams of treasure buried in the forest. He had been picked up with the other ruffians in Jondrette's garret, but his well-attested drunkenness that night saved him: the courts could not tell whether he was a robber or a victim, dropped the charge, and he went back to breaking stones on the Gagny–Lagny road, his taste for theft somewhat cooled and his taste for wine undiminished.

One morning before daybreak he sees through the branches a man whose back and shoulders seem familiar, though he cannot place him; he recalls only that many years before a man had given him the same uneasy feeling. The stranger has clearly walked all night from Paris, with no bundle. Boulatruelle thinks of the treasure, takes his sharp pickaxe, and follows the trail of footprints and bent branches. When the track fails he climbs a great beech and spots his man slipping into a distant glade he knows well, the Blaru-bottom, marked by a heap of porous stones and an ailing chestnut-tree bandaged with a sheet of zinc nailed to its bark.

He drops from the tree and, trusting the straight line through the brambles rather than the winding paths, takes forty minutes to reach the glade, scratched, soaked and furious. The man is gone. The heap of stones is in place, but behind it, before the zinc-plastered tree, lies freshly turned earth, a pickaxe left behind, and a hole. The hole is empty. 'Thief!' Boulatruelle shrieks at the horizon.

title: Marius, Emerging from Civil War, Makes Ready for Domestic War
summary: Marius lies for months between life and death at his grandfather's, visited daily by a well-dressed white-haired stranger who leaves lint; as he recovers, M. Gillenormand is transfigured by joy, while Marius, thinking only of Cosette, stays cold and prepares for a battle over his marriage.
details: For weeks after the night of the barricade Marius lies in fever and delirium at the Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire, repeating Cosette's name, his head wounds and suppurating lesions a constant danger. The doctor forbids all emotion. Every day, sometimes twice, a very well-dressed gentleman with white hair calls at the porter's lodge to ask after the wounded man and leaves a large package of lint for the dressings. On the 7th of September, four months to the day, the doctor answers for Marius's life; two more months on a long chair follow because of his broken collarbone. The long illness also shields him from prosecution: public indignation at the order requiring doctors to inform on the wounded, shared by the King himself, means the councils of war leave the insurgents who were not taken in arms alone.

M. Gillenormand passes from anguish to ecstasy. He has his armchair carried to the bedside, insists on the finest linen for lint, cries 'Aïe!' when dead flesh is cut away, and asks the doctor the same questions over and over. On the day Marius is pronounced out of danger he gives the porter three louis, dances a gavotte, sings a bawdy song, and is seen by Basque kneeling on a chair in prayer, he who had never believed in God. He sends a bouquet to a pretty neighbour, calls Marius 'M. le Baron', shouts 'Long live the Republic!', and becomes, in Hugo's phrase, the grandson of his grandson.

Marius, meanwhile, has one fixed idea: Cosette. He does not know what has become of her, remembers the barricade as a cloud of shadows (Éponine, Gavroche, Mabeuf, the Thénardiers, his friends), finds the passage of M. Fauchelevent through it a puzzle, and has no idea how or by whom he was saved; all anyone can tell him is that he was brought home at night in a hackney-coach. He is barely softened by his grandfather's tenderness, distrusts it as a ploy, and never once calls him 'father'. As his strength returns so does the memory of his father's wrongs. He tests the ground by praising the men of '93; the old man falls silent all day, which Marius reads as suppressed wrath. He resolves that if he is refused he will tear off his bandages and refuse food: he will have Cosette or die.

title: Marius Attacked
summary: When Marius announces that he wishes to marry, his grandfather instantly agrees, reveals that he has already found Cosette through the old gentleman who calls every day, and the two weep in each other's arms; Marius calls him 'father' for the first time.
details: One day, as M. Gillenormand gently recommends a cutlet rather than fried sole, Marius gathers all his strength, sits up, fixes him with a terrible look and declares: 'I wish to marry.' 'Agreed,' says the grandfather, and bursts out laughing. He has made his inquiries: the girl comes every day in the shape of an old gentleman to ask after Marius, she has spent the time weeping and making lint, she lives at No. 7 Rue de l'Homme Armé, the story about the lancer was false, she is a jewel. He had thought of simply planting her at the bedside, but that is only done in novels. 'Take her. Such is my ferocity.' He confesses he saw that Marius did not love him and hoped that giving him Cosette would make him love him a little.

The old man dissolves into sobs, clasps Marius's head to his breast, and both weep. 'Father!' cries Marius; 'Ah, so you love me!' answers the grandfather. Marius asks whether he may see her; tomorrow, says the old man, then today, since Marius has said 'father' three times and it is worth it.

The chapter ends in comedy. The grandfather quotes André Chénier, blunders into saying his throat was cut by 'the ras... by the giants of '93', sees a frown on Marius's face, tries to retract and tangles himself hopelessly, and rushes purple-faced from the room to seize Basque by the collar in the anteroom and bellow that 'those ruffians did assassinate him!' 'Who, sir?' 'André Chénier!' 'Yes, sir,' says Basque in alarm.

title: Mademoiselle Gillenormand Ends by No Longer Thinking It a Bad Thing That M. Fauchelevent Should Have Entered with Something Under His Arm
summary: Cosette is brought to Marius's room with 'M. Fauchelevent', whom the narrator names as Jean Valjean; the grandfather asks for her hand on Marius's behalf, and when he laments that the couple will be poor after his death, Valjean announces that Mademoiselle Euphrasie Fauchelevent has six hundred thousand francs and lays a bundle of banknotes on the table.
details: Cosette enters Marius's chamber before the whole household, including Basque and Nicolette, and the grandfather, caught mid-way through blowing his nose, exclaims 'Adorable!' She is frightened and in heaven, longing to throw herself into Marius's arms and not daring. Behind her comes a grave white-haired man with a heartrending smile, 'Monsieur Fauchelevent': the narrator says plainly that it is Jean Valjean, in new black clothes and a white cravat. The porter is far from recognising in this correct bourgeois the mud-covered, bloodied man who brought Marius home on the night of the 7th of June, though something about the face nags at him. Valjean stands apart by the door with a mouldy-looking package under his arm that Mademoiselle Gillenormand takes for a book.

M. Gillenormand, careless with names, bows to 'Monsieur Tranchelevent' and asks on behalf of his grandson, Baron Marius Pontmercy, for the hand of Mademoiselle. The other bows. 'Permission to adore each other!' The lovers chatter in low voices: Cosette scolds him for going to fight, tells him she has been dead for four months, that they still live in the Rue de l'Homme Armé with no garden, and shows the callus on her fingers from making lint. The grandfather tells everyone else to make a noise so the children can talk, and lectures Cosette on marriage, churches and the folly of spinsterhood. Asked about his close friend, Marius names Courfeyrac and says he is dead; 'That is good,' says the grandfather absently. Aunt Gillenormand watches this irruption of light into her failed life with stupefied innocence.

Taking all four hands in his, the old man suddenly turns gloomy: more than half his fortune is in an annuity, and after his death the children will not have a sou. A grave, tranquil voice answers from behind them: 'Mademoiselle Euphrasie Fauchelevent possesses six hundred thousand francs.' 'I am she,' says Cosette. Jean Valjean opens the package: five hundred thousand-franc notes and one hundred and sixty-eight of five hundred, five hundred and eighty-four thousand francs in all. 'This is a fine book,' says M. Gillenormand, and jokes that Marius has found a millionaire grisette in his tree of dreams, while the aunt murmurs the sum over and over. Marius and Cosette, gazing at each other, scarcely notice.

title: Deposit Your Money in a Forest Rather Than with a Notary
summary: The narrator explains that the fortune is the money Jean Valjean withdrew from Laffitte as M. Madeleine and buried, with the Bishop's candlesticks, in the Blaru-bottom at Montfermeil; he was the man Boulatruelle saw, and he now knows from the newspapers that Javert has been found drowned.
details: Hugo ties up the forest mystery. After the Champmathieu affair, during his first brief escape, Jean Valjean reached Paris and withdrew from Laffitte's bank the six hundred and thirty thousand francs he had earned at Montreuil-sur-Mer under the name of Madeleine. Fearing recapture, which indeed followed, he buried the banknotes in a box packed in a coffer of chestnut shavings in the forest of Montfermeil, in the glade called the Blaru-bottom, and with them the Bishop's candlesticks, which he had carried off when he fled Montreuil-sur-Mer. The man Boulatruelle once saw in the forest at evening was Valjean; so was the man he saw at dawn in the last chapter. Whenever he needed money he went to the Blaru-bottom, which accounts for the absences mentioned earlier. Seeing Marius convalescent and the moment at hand, he dug up the whole sum and left Boulatruelle his pickaxe.

The actual sum was five hundred and eighty-four thousand five hundred francs; Valjean kept back five hundred for himself, thinking 'We shall see hereafter.' The difference from the original six hundred and thirty thousand represents ten years of expenses from 1823 to 1833, the five years in the convent having cost only five thousand francs. He sets the two candlesticks on his chimneypiece, where Toussaint admires them.

He also knows that he is delivered from Javert. The story has been told in his hearing and he has checked it in the Moniteur: a police inspector named Javert was found drowned under a laundry-boat between the Pont au Change and the Pont-Neuf, and a paper he left behind, from a man otherwise irreproachable and esteemed by his superiors, pointed to mental derangement and suicide. 'In fact,' Valjean thinks, 'since he let me go once he had me in his power, he must already have been mad.'

title: The Two Old Men Do Everything, Each One After His Own Fashion, to Render Cosette Happy
summary: The wedding is fixed for February; Jean Valjean builds Cosette a legal identity as Euphrasie Fauchelevent, orphan of the 'other' Fauchelevent and heiress to an anonymous legacy, while M. Gillenormand showers her with heirlooms and holds forth on the lost art of festivity; the aunt, reconciled by the half-million, decides to leave the couple her fortune.
details: The doctor allows the wedding for February; it is now December, and weeks of perfect happiness pass. Marius and Cosette have gone from the sepulchre to paradise without transition and understand nothing of it; Cosette thinks the good God is looking after them. Jean Valjean smooths every difficulty. Having been a mayor, he knows how to solve the problem only he understands, Cosette's civil status: he invents for her a family of dead people. She is the daughter not of himself but of the other Fauchelevent, his brother, both once gardeners at the Petit-Picpus; the nuns, never clear which Fauchelevent she belonged to, give glowing references, and an acte de notoriété makes her legally Mademoiselle Euphrasie Fauchelevent, orphan. Valjean, as Fauchelevent, is appointed her guardian, with M. Gillenormand supervising. The five hundred and eighty-odd thousand francs become a legacy from a dead benefactor who wished to remain unknown, reduced from five hundred and ninety-four thousand by the cost of her education. The oddities go unnoticed, one party blinded by love and the others by the money.

Cosette learns that the old man she has so long called father is only a kinsman. At any other time it would have broken her heart; now it is a faint passing cloud, for she has Marius, and she has long been used to enigmas around her. She goes on calling him father nonetheless. She is enchanted by Father Gillenormand, who rifles his lacquered chests for Binche guipure, lace, moiré, India kerchiefs and antique jewels, adds a tea-rose moiré antique gown after Marius calls the revolutionaries 'antique memories', and expounds his philosophy of the superfluous: happiness is only the necessary, and dry happiness is dry bread. He delivers a vast tirade on how the nineteenth century has forgotten how to marry, with garters, violins under the trees, Dryads and Nereids.

Aunt Gillenormand surveys it all with placidity; the six hundred thousand francs were her last surprise. Piqued that her father never consulted her about the marriage, she had reserved the question of her inheritance, and would likely have left a poor nephew poor; but one owes consideration to six hundred thousand francs, so she will leave her fortune to the young people, who do not need it. The couple are to live with the grandfather, who gives up his own chamber, hangs it with buttercup satin he says once draped a duchess's bed, and turns his library into the lawyer's study the Order requires of Marius.

title: The Effects of Dreams Mingled with Happiness
summary: Cosette visits daily with M. Fauchelevent, who barely speaks to Marius; Marius, with a four-month gap in his memory, begins to doubt he ever saw Fauchelevent at the barricade, and when Fauchelevent denies knowing the Rue de la Chanvrerie, concludes he was hallucinating.
details: The lovers meet every day, Cosette chaperoned by M. Fauchelevent, which Mademoiselle Gillenormand finds backwards: the bride coming to court. Marius and Fauchelevent see each other but hardly speak; Fauchelevent is the condition attached to Cosette and Marius accepts him. They edge towards conversation only on general politics and once, on free and compulsory education, nearly agree. Fauchelevent talks well, even loftily, yet lacks something indefinable: something less and something more than a man of the world.

Marius surrounds this cold, benevolent man with silent questions. Four months of agony have dug a black hole in his memory, and he has reached the point of wondering whether he really saw so calm and serious a man in the barricade. Other ghosts trouble him too: Mabeuf falling, Gavroche singing in the grapeshot, Éponine's cold brow under his lips, Enjolras, Courfeyrac, Prouvaire, Combeferre, Bossuet, Grantaire rising and dispersing like smoke. Were they dreams? Is he the same man, the poor man now rich, the abandoned man now with a family, who entered a tomb black and came out white while the others stayed inside?

Fauchelevent almost belongs among these vanished beings, and Marius half decides the Fauchelevent of the barricade was a nightmare of his delirium. Both men are too rigid for a direct question. Once only Marius tries, mentioning the Rue de la Chanvrerie and asking, 'Of course you know that street?' 'I have no idea of the name of that street,' Fauchelevent replies in the most natural manner. The answer, which bears on the name and not the street, strikes Marius as more conclusive than it is. 'Decidedly,' he thinks, 'I have been dreaming. M. Fauchelevent was not there.'

title: Two Men Impossible to Find
summary: Marius searches for the two men he owes: Thénardier, now condemned to death in his absence and vanished (his wife having died in prison), and the unknown man who carried him through the sewer, of whom only a coachman's tale and a torn coat remain; when Marius vows he would give Cosette's fortune to find his saviour, Jean Valjean says nothing.
details: Before entering joyfully into the future Marius wants a quittance from the past. He owes two debts of gratitude, one for his father and one for himself: to Thénardier, who saved Colonel Pontmercy at Waterloo (Marius does not know the real scene there, and that his father owed Thénardier his life without owing him thanks), and to the unknown man who brought him home. His agents find no trace of Thénardier. Madame Thénardier has died in prison awaiting trial; Thénardier and his daughter Azelma have sunk back into the dark. The Gorbeau ambush case has collapsed: with Claquesous vanished and the chief accused escaped, the Assizes could only sentence two underlings, Panchaud alias Bigrenaille and Demi-Liard, to ten years in the galleys; the fugitives got hard labour for life in their absence, and Thénardier, as ringleader, was condemned to death in absentia, which drives him deeper into hiding.

The search for his rescuer begins well and stops dead. The hackney-coachman is found: on the 6th of June, on a police agent's orders, he waited from three in the afternoon until nightfall on the Quai des Champs-Élysées above the outlet of the Grand Sewer; towards nine the grating opened and a man came out carrying another who seemed dead; the agent arrested the living man and seized the body; they drove to the Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire and left the dead man, who was Marius, then on near the Archives, where the agent paid the coachman and led the other man away. Marius remembers only a hand seizing him from behind as he fell in the barricade. Someone carried him from the Halles to the Champs-Élysées through the sewer. Who?

The prefecture knows nothing of any arrest at the sewer mouth on the 6th of June and treats the coachman's story as a fable invented for a tip. Yet Marius cannot doubt it without doubting his own existence. Why does this man give no sign? Did he escape the agent? Is he dead? Basque and Nicolette saw only their bleeding master; the porter, the only witness, can say just that 'that man was terrible.' Marius keeps his bloodstained clothes in case they help; one skirt of the coat has a piece torn away.

One evening, before Cosette and Jean Valjean, Marius describes the fruitless search and, irritated by 'Monsieur Fauchelevent's' cold face, exclaims that the man was sublime, an archangel who carried a corpse a league and a half through the sewers for the sake of a spark of life, and was arrested for it. 'Oh, if Cosette's six hundred thousand francs were mine...' 'They are yours,' Valjean interrupts. 'Well, I would give them all to find that man again.' Jean Valjean remains silent.

title: The 16th of February, 1833
summary: Marius and Cosette marry on Shrove Tuesday, 1833, at the Gillenormand house, after Jean Valjean hands over the fortune and, pleading a crushed thumb, avoids signing the papers; on the way to Saint-Paul the wedding carriages halt beside a cartload of maskers, among whom an old 'Spaniard' recognises the man with his arm in a sling and orders his daughter Azelma to find out where the wedding goes.
details: The night of the 16th to 17th of February 1833 is the wedding night of Marius and Cosette, and Hugo opens with a mock-elegy for the old fashion of marrying at home, before France learned from England to flee in a post-chaise. The banns and papers could not be ready before the 16th, which fell on Shrove Tuesday; the aunt hesitates, the grandfather quotes a proverb promising that a Mardi Gras marriage has no ungrateful children, and the day is kept despite the public merrymaking. It rains. The evening before, Jean Valjean handed Marius the five hundred and eighty-four thousand francs in M. Gillenormand's presence; the marriage being under community of property, the papers were simple. Toussaint passes to Cosette as lady's maid, and a fine chamber in the Gillenormand house is furnished for Valjean, whom Cosette has almost made promise to occupy it.

A few days before the wedding Valjean crushed the thumb of his right hand, would let no one dress or even see the hurt, and has carried the arm in a sling ever since, which prevents him from signing; M. Gillenormand, as supervising guardian, signed in his place. Repaving blocks the direct road to Saint-Paul, so the carriages turn through the boulevard among the Carnival crowds, the grandfather delighted that the young folk will see 'a bit of the masquerade'. The first coach carries Cosette, Aunt Gillenormand, M. Gillenormand and Jean Valjean; Marius, by custom, follows in the second. Hugo digresses on the cartloads of maskers, their ancient tradition and the suspicious, government-sponsored laughter of the Carnival.

At the Pont-aux-Choux both files of vehicles stop, and a calash full of maskers halts opposite the bride's carriage. Two of them, an old 'Spaniard' with a huge nose and black moustache and a gaunt young fishwife in a half-mask, talk under the uproar. The Spaniard is certain he knows 'that old cove' in the first carriage with his arm 'hung up in a black cravat', and guesses from his place that he is the bride's father. He wants the girl to jump down and follow the wedding; she cannot, because she is hired for the day by the prefecture and would be arrested if she left the cart, and he himself can only go out masked and must go back into his hole on Ash Wednesday. He insists she find out what that wedding is, whom the old man belongs to and where the couple live. 'You understand me, Azelma.' The files move on and the maskers lose sight of the bride's 'trap'.

title: Jean Valjean Still Wears His Arm in a Sling
summary: The wedding day: the grandfather gives Cosette away in Valjean's place, the couple return radiant to the Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire, and at the banquet Jean Valjean's armchair stands empty; he has slipped away pleading his injured hand, Marius takes his seat beside Cosette, and the grandfather delivers a long toast to love.
details: Cosette, dressed by Toussaint and Nicolette in white taffeta, Binche guipure, English point, pearls and orange blossom, is dazzling at the mayor's office and at church; beneath Marius's curls the pale scars of the barricade show. The grandfather, resplendent in the elegance of the Barras era, escorts the bride, taking the place of Jean Valjean, whose arm is still in its sling. Valjean follows them in black, smiling, while M. Gillenormand decrees joy and the abolition of unhappiness. After the vows, the registers, the rings and the white moiré pall, the couple emerge hand in hand, Cosette still unable to believe it is real. In the carriage home the grandfather hails 'Monsieur le Baron and Madame la Baronne, with an income of thirty thousand livres', and Cosette whispers to Marius, 'My name is Marius. I am Madame Thou.' They promise each other to go back and look at their little garden in the Rue Plumet.

At the Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire Marius climbs, triumphant, the staircase up which he was carried dying; the poor at the door bless them; flowers are everywhere. Captain Théodule Gillenormand has come from Chartres for his cousin's wedding; Cosette does not recognise him and he remembers her no more than any other woman, so the grandfather congratulates himself on never having believed the lancer story. Cosette has never been more tender with Jean Valjean, speaking to him in the inflections of her childhood. Before dinner she finds him on a chair half hidden behind the drawing-room door, curtsies deeply in her bridal dress, and asks, 'Father, are you satisfied?' 'Yes, I am content.' 'Well, then, laugh.' And Jean Valjean laughs.

In the brilliant dining-room, with its Venetian chandelier of coloured glass birds and a Haydn quartet playing in the antechamber, two armchairs flank the bride: one for M. Gillenormand, one for Jean Valjean. The second stays empty. Basque reports that M. Fauchelevent asked him to say his injured hand was paining him, that he could not dine with the Baron and Baroness, begged to be excused and would come tomorrow, and has just left. The empty chair chills the table for a moment; then the grandfather, beaming for two, gives the seat to Marius, 'Fortunatus beside Fortunata', and Cosette, saddened at first, is soon content to have her husband beside her and sets her white satin foot on his. Within five minutes the whole table is laughing with the animation of forgetfulness.

At dessert the grandfather rises with a half-filled glass and delivers his sermon: adore each other, give rein to your joys, down with the philosophers who preach moderation; woman is the one royalty no revolution has toppled; love is six thousand years old and still new; be Daphnis and Chloe while waiting to become Philemon and Baucis. The evening is gay, there is dancing, and a little after midnight the married pair disappear and the Gillenormand house becomes a temple. Hugo pauses on the threshold of the wedding night with a meditation on love as the one true happiness.

title: The Inseparable
summary: Jean Valjean leaves the wedding unnoticed, listens for a while beneath the lighted windows, and walks home to the empty flat in the Rue de l'Homme Armé, where he takes off the sling, opens the little valise Cosette called his 'inseparable', lays out the mourning clothes she wore as a child leaving Montfermeil, and weeps over them.
details: Immediately after laughing at Cosette's command, while no one is watching, Jean Valjean rises and slips into the antechamber, the very room he entered eight months earlier black with mud and blood, carrying the grandson to the grandfather; now the musicians sit on the sofa where Marius was laid down, and Basque in knee-breeches arranges roses round the dishes. Valjean points to his sling, charges Basque to explain his absence, and goes out. He stands for several minutes in the dark beneath the radiant dining-room windows, listening to the grandfather's voice, the violins, the plates, the laughter, and through it all Cosette's sweet, joyous voice.

He walks back to the Rue de l'Homme Armé by the slightly longer way through the Rue Saint-Louis and the Blancs-Manteaux, the road he has taken every day for three months because Cosette passed along it. The apartment is empty; even Toussaint is gone. The cupboards stand open. In Cosette's room the bed is stripped, the pillow bare, all her small feminine belongings carried away; only one bed in the flat is made up, his own. He wanders from room to room closing cupboard doors, then sets his candle in his chamber. He takes his arm out of the sling and uses the right hand as if it did not hurt at all.

His eyes fall on the little portmanteau that never leaves him, the 'inseparable' of which Cosette was jealous, set on a round table by his bed since the 4th of June. He unlocks it and slowly draws out the clothes in which, ten years before, Cosette left Montfermeil: the little gown, the black fichu, the stout coarse shoes, the thick fustian bodice, the knitted petticoat, the apron with pockets, the woollen stockings no longer than his hand, all black. He had brought those mourning clothes to Montfermeil for her himself, that cold December when she shivered in rags with red feet in wooden shoes, and he remembers walking through the leafless forest hand in hand with a child who had no one in the world but him, her big doll in her arms and a louis d'or in her apron pocket. He lays the garments out on the bed, looks at them one by one, and then his white head falls forward into them and that stoical old heart breaks; anyone on the stairs would have heard frightful sobs.

title: The Immortal Liver 112
summary: Through the whole winter night Jean Valjean wrestles for the last time with his conscience over what he is to do with the happiness he has built: cling to Cosette and bring his hidden past into the Gillenormand household, or let go and sink alone; by dawn he is still prostrate over her little clothes, and the chapter does not say what he decides.
details: The old, formidable struggle begins again. Jacob wrestled with the angel for one night; Hugo recalls how many times Jean Valjean has been seized by his conscience in the dark, overthrown by the truth, dazzled against his will by the spark the Bishop lit in him, and left at the end bleeding but at peace. Tonight he feels he is passing through his final combat. Once more two roads open before him, one tempting and one alarming, the terrible port and the smiling ambush, and the mysterious finger in the darkness points him to the one that alarms him.

The question is this: how is he to behave towards the happiness of Cosette and Marius? He willed it and made it; they have everything, even riches, and it is his doing. But must he now force himself on that happiness? Remain the half-seen, respected father he has been? Bring his past, unspoken, to their future, and seat himself veiled at that bright fireside, placing feet that drag the shadow of the law on the Gillenormand fender? Be the silent mute of destiny beside two happy beings? Cosette is the raft of his shipwreck: if he clings to it he is saved and lives; if he lets go, the abyss.

He fights, now against his will, now against his conviction, and the past surges up before the present. Hugo pleads on his behalf: is there no limit to the obedience of the soul, can perpetual self-sacrifice be exacted, who would blame Sisyphus or Jean Valjean for saying 'It is enough'? What was the Champmathieu affair beside this; what is a return to the galleys beside entrance into the void? Martyrdom has its throne, crown and sceptre of red-hot iron, but the mantle of flame still remains to be put on. At last he reaches the peace of exhaustion and weighs the two sacrifices, Cosette's or his own.

What he resolves the chapter does not say. He stays until daylight bent double over the bed, arms flung out like a man unnailed from a cross and thrown face down, twelve hours of a winter night, ice-cold, motionless as a corpse, his thoughts crawling and soaring. Once he shudders and his mouth, pressed to Cosette's garments, kisses them, and so one sees he is alive. Who could see? No one was there, except the One who is in the shadows.

title: The Seventh Circle and the Eighth Heaven
summary: The morning after the wedding Jean Valjean asks to see Marius alone, unwinds the bandage to show an uninjured thumb, and tells him he is an ex-convict named Jean Valjean, nineteen years in the galleys and now a fugitive, and no relation of Cosette's; Marius promises to keep the secret, coldly agrees it is better he not see Cosette, then relents and tells him to come every evening.
details: A little past midday on the 17th of February, Basque admits M. Fauchelevent to the disordered drawing-room, where fallen flowers and guttered candles still speak of the feast. Valjean asks that his name not be announced. He is deathly pale, hollow-eyed, his coat creased from a night without sleep. Marius bounds in, radiant and sleepless too, and calls him 'father' for the first time, pouring out plans: they will have no more of the Rue de l'Homme Armé; his chamber here is ready, facing south on the garden, with a nightingale in the acacias, a place of honour for the little valise, whist with the grandfather, walks with Cosette as in the Luxembourg days. 'Sir,' says Jean Valjean, 'I have something to say to you. I am an ex-convict.'

Marius cannot take the words in. Valjean unties the black cravat, unrolls the linen from his hand and shows the thumb: there was never anything wrong with it; he invented the injury so as not to sign and put a forgery into the marriage papers. He was nineteen years in the galleys for theft, then condemned for life as a second offender, and has broken his ban. Marius, horrified, cries, 'You are Cosette's father!' Valjean draws himself up: before God, no. He is a peasant of Faverolles, a pruner of trees; his name is not Fauchelevent but Jean Valjean; he is nothing to Cosette, a passer-by who ten years ago did not know she existed, who took in an orphan who needed him. Cosette now passes out of his life into a better providence. The six hundred thousand francs were a deposit, and he restores it, completing the restitution by giving his true name.

Pressed by Marius as to why he confesses when no one pursues him, Valjean answers: out of honesty, and because of a thread in his heart he could not break. He could have stayed Monsieur Fauchelevent, had the chamber, lived as one family; and at that word he becomes wild. He belongs to no family. To keep silent would have been a lie lived every day, the galleys introduced to their fireside, Cosette condemned to him forever, three heads in the green cap. Conscience is a grasp like a fist in his own collar: 'I am tracked. By whom? By myself.' Fauchelevent could lend him his name but he could not take it; a name is an I; in days gone by he stole a loaf to live, today to live he will not steal a name. He points to his dragging leg: 'Now you understand why.' And he asks Marius to imagine the police one day tearing off the mask in front of them all. Marius, convinced, offers a hand that Valjean does not offer back, and promises to procure his pardon through the grandfather's friends; Valjean says it is useless, he is believed dead, and the only pardon he needs is his conscience's.

Cosette, in a voluminous white dressing-gown, puts her head round the door, accuses them of talking politics on the morning after a wedding, demands a kiss from her father (who gives her the smile of a spectre) and is sent away by Marius with talk of investing her six hundred thousand francs. When she is gone Marius murmurs, 'Poor Cosette, when she finds out...', and Valjean, trembling, begs him on his most sacred word never to tell her; she saw the chain-gang pass once. He weeps silently, murmuring that he wishes he could die. Marius promises to keep the secret for himself alone, and, with cooling distance, offers a recompense for the honestly returned deposit, which Valjean gently declines. Then Valjean asks whether he ought not to see Cosette any more; 'I think that would be better,' Marius says coldly. 'I shall never see her more,' Valjean murmurs, reaches the door, and turns back livid: if he had not wished to go on seeing Cosette he would simply have gone away; it was in order to stay near her that he had to tell the truth. He asks to come rarely, briefly, by the ordinary door, to be received in the little ground-floor waiting-room at nightfall. 'You shall come every evening,' says Marius, 'and Cosette will be waiting for you.' Happiness escorts despair to the door.

title: The Obscurities Which a Revelation Can Contain
summary: Marius turns the confession over: the returned fortune and the voluntary avowal argue for an awakening conscience, but he concludes that Valjean fled the Gorbeau ambush because he was a fugitive, went to the barricade to take revenge on Javert and killed him, and he recoils from the convict while realising he dared not ask the decisive questions.
details: Marius is upset. The estrangement he always felt towards the man beside Cosette is explained: M. Fauchelevent is the convict Jean Valjean, a scorpion found in a nest of turtledoves. Has he wedded the convict as well? He asks whether he has anything to reproach himself with and admits his dreamy, visionary side: in the six or seven ecstatic weeks of the Rue Plumet he never even told Cosette about the Gorbeau drama or named the Thénardiers or Éponine, half out of intoxication and half out of a dull instinct to bury an adventure in which he could only have been an accuser. Yet had he known everything, would he have loved or married her any less? No. Love bandaged his eyes to lead him to paradise, though that paradise now has an infernal accompaniment.

His horror is mixed with pity and surprise. This twice-convicted thief restored a deposit of six hundred thousand francs that he alone knew of; he revealed himself when nothing forced him, rejecting the shelter of a false name, out of a scruple of conscience. Whatever he is, he is a conscience awakening, and his sincerity makes inquiry useless. Strange reversal: M. Fauchelevent inspired distrust, Jean Valjean inspires confidence. But the cloud returns. Why did that man flee the police at the Jondrette garret instead of lodging a complaint? Because he was a fugitive who had broken his ban. Why had he come to the barricade? Marius now distinctly remembers Valjean dragging the bound Javert out of the barricade and the pistol shot behind the corner of the Rue Mondétour. Obviously there was hatred between the spy and the galley-slave; Valjean went there for vengeance and, Marius concludes, killed Javert.

One question has no answer: how did this man's life come to run alongside Cosette's for so long? What bound the lamb to the wolf, and, stranger still, the wolf to the lamb, so that for nine years the angel had the monster as her support? Marius sees in this Jean Valjean's secret and also God's: the workman was horrible, the work admirable; the dung-heap has helped the spring make the rose before. He clings to the declaration 'I am nothing to Cosette', decides Valjean's part is finished and that he, Marius, is now Cosette's providence, and still returns to horror. On penal questions Marius, democrat though he is, holds the inexorable view that a convict is lower than the lowest rung, and his final gesture is to turn away his head.

Hugo insists on one thing: Marius did not put the two or three decisive questions (the Jondrette attic, the barricade, Javert) because he was afraid of the answers and of where a hideous glare might reach, perhaps to Cosette. He already knew too much and preferred to dull his senses. He now regrets the promise he let himself be drawn into; he should simply have rejected the man and freed his house of him. Still, one must keep one's word even to a convict. He hides his trouble from Cosette and, questioning her casually about her childhood, becomes ever more convinced that this convict was everything good and paternal a man could be to her: the sinister nettle had loved and protected the lily.

title: The Lower Chamber
summary: The next evening Jean Valjean comes and asks to be received in a damp, cobwebbed ground-floor room; Cosette scolds and coaxes, but he refuses her kisses, insists she call him 'Monsieur Jean' and addresses her as 'you' and 'Madame', until her innocent question whether he is angry because she is happy breaks his guard for a moment.
details: At nightfall Basque is waiting in the courtyard, as though on orders, to ask whether monsieur wishes to go upstairs or remain below. 'I will remain below.' The waiting-room is a small vaulted cellar paved with red tiles and lit by a grated window, with a black spider's web wheel on one pane, a heap of empty bottles in a corner, a flaking ochre wall and a narrow black chimneypiece where, tellingly, a fire has already been lit: his answer was foreseen. Two armchairs and a threadbare rug stand by the hearth. Valjean, who has neither eaten nor slept for days, sinks into a chair and does not notice Basque bring a candle.

Suddenly Cosette is beside him. She knows he is peculiar but never expected this; Marius told her he wished to be received here. She demands a kiss and offers her cheek, then, quoting Christ, the other; he does not move, as if nailed to the floor. She orders him upstairs to dine; impossible. He slips into 'thou', catches himself, and says, 'You know, madame, that I am peculiar.' Madame! She is to call him 'Monsieur Jean', or 'Jean'; since she is Madame Pontmercy he can be Monsieur Jean. Bewildered and hurt, she presses his hands to her neck and begs him to be good, which means coming to live with them, leaving the Rue de l'Homme Armé, and being her father. 'You no longer need a father, you have a husband.' He takes refuge in Toussaint's authority for his old ways and changes the subject to a pretty rosewood toilet table he saw in a shop window, and she blows at him like an angry cat.

She rages that everyone has been tormenting her since yesterday, that her carefully arranged chamber is left on her hands, that he wants to be received in a cellar where the walls have beards. Then, suddenly serious: 'Are you angry with me because I am happy?' The question, simple for her, lacerates him. He turns pale and murmurs, half to himself, that her happiness was the object of his life, that God may sign his dismissal, 'Cosette, thou art happy; my day is over.' 'Ah, you have said thou to me!' She springs to his neck and he strains her wildly to him as if taking her back, then gently detaches her arms, takes his hat, and from the threshold says: 'I have said thou to you. Tell your husband that this shall not happen again. Pardon me.' He leaves Cosette stupefied by this enigmatic farewell.

title: Another Step Backwards
summary: Jean Valjean comes every evening at the same hour; Cosette, soothed by Marius, stops questioning and accepts 'Monsieur Jean' and 'Madame', the household settles on calling him an original, and he gradually detaches her from himself, so that when she once slips and says 'father' he corrects her and hides his tears.
details: The next day Valjean returns at the same hour and Cosette asks nothing, no longer complains of the cold or the cellar, avoids both 'father' and 'Monsieur Jean', and lets herself be called 'you' and 'Madame'; only her joy is slightly dimmed. She has evidently had with Marius one of those conversations in which the beloved man explains nothing and satisfies the beloved woman. Basque has removed the bottles and Nicolette the spiders. Valjean comes every day because he cannot take Marius's words other than literally; Marius arranges to be out at those hours. The house grows used to 'M. Fauchelevent's' ways: Toussaint says monsieur has always been like that, and the grandfather, who at ninety-six wants no new attachments, settles the matter with 'He's an original', citing a marquis who bought a palace to live in its garret.

No one glimpses the sinister foundation. Hugo compares such a man to an Indian marsh that ripples without wind, a surface disturbed by a hydra on the bottom; many men carry a secret dragon, and the small singularities of the solitary, the side door, the deserted street, the candle left at the porter's lodge, often proceed from a formidable depth.

Weeks pass. Cosette's new life fills with visits, housekeeping and, above all, being with Marius, walking arm in arm with him in the open street before the whole world. Toussaint cannot get on with Nicolette and leaves. Valjean comes every day. The 'you', the 'Madame', the 'Monsieur Jean' make him another person to her; the care he has taken to detach her is succeeding, and she becomes gayer and less tender, though she still loves him and he feels it. One day she says: you were my father, then my uncle, then Monsieur Fauchelevent, now Jean; who are you? If I did not know how good you are I should be afraid of you. He still lives in the Rue de l'Homme Armé because he cannot bear to move away from her quarter, and as the days lengthen his visits grow longer. Once she chances to call him 'father'; a flash of joy lights his face and he catches her up: 'Say Jean.' 'Ah! truly, Monsieur Jean,' she laughs. 'That is right,' he says, and turns away so she will not see him wipe his eyes.

title: They Recall the Garden of the Rue Plumet
summary: Marius and Cosette revisit their garden in the Rue Plumet and Valjean waits in vain; he notices the couple's strict economy and that the fire, then the armchairs, vanish from the lower room, understands he is being shown the door, and stops coming, sending word that he is busy and about to travel.
details: That was the last time; after that flash, extinction. Valjean has lost Cosette wholly in one day and must now lose her again in detail, yet his whole life is concentrated in the daily hour when he sits beside her and talks of her childhood, the convent and her little friends. One warm afternoon in early April Marius proposes they go back to their garden in the Rue Plumet, whose lease still belongs to Cosette, and they fly off like two swallows; that evening Basque tells Valjean that Madame has gone out with Monsieur and has not returned. He waits an hour and leaves with drooping head. Next day Cosette talks of nothing but having 'lived a whole day in her past' and does not notice she missed him.

Valjean has observed the young couple's severe economy and is troubled. Why no carriage of their own, when a coupé costs only five hundred francs a month? Why has Toussaint not been replaced? 'Have I not Marius?' says Cosette. He urges her to profit by her riches; she does not answer. To prolong his visits he praises Marius, and she outdoes him; Basque has to come twice to say dinner is served. One day there is no fire in the hearth; he tells himself it is April. Cosette exclaims at the cold and learns he told Basque not to light it 'since it is May'; next day there is a fire but the armchairs have been moved to the far end by the door, and he carries them back. Then Cosette reports something odd her husband said: of their thirty thousand livres, twenty-seven are hers and three his grandfather's; would she have the courage to live on the three? She said yes, on nothing, with him.

Valjean finds no word to answer and, walking home, enters the wrong house and climbs two floors before noticing. He concludes that Marius doubts the origin of the six hundred thousand francs, perhaps has even discovered it comes from him, and would rather be poor than rich on unclean money; and he begins to sense that he is being shown the door. The next day the armchairs are gone altogether, and he stammers that he himself told Basque to remove them because he can only stay a few minutes. Cosette shrugs at his oddities. 'Adieu!' he murmurs, unable to say either 'Adieu, Cosette' or 'Adieu, Madame'. This time he has understood.

He does not come the next day; Cosette notices only in the evening and is at once diverted by a kiss. Nor the day after. She sends Nicolette to ask whether he is ill: M. Jean replies that he is not ill but busy, will come soon, is about to take one of his little journeys, and they are not to think of him. Nicolette repeats that Madame wants to know why he did not come 'yesterday evening'. 'It is two days since I have been there,' Valjean says gently; the remark goes unnoticed and unreported.

title: Attraction and Extinction
summary: Through the spring and summer of 1833 an old man in black walks every evening from the Rue de l'Homme Armé towards the Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire, peers round the corner weeping, and turns back; day by day his walk grows shorter, like a pendulum running down, until he no longer passes the Blancs-Manteaux.
details: In the last months of spring and the first of summer 1833 the shopkeepers and loungers of the Marais notice an old man neatly dressed in black who comes out of the Rue de l'Homme Armé every day towards nightfall, passes the Blancs-Manteaux and the Rue Culture-Sainte-Catherine, and turns into the Rue Saint-Louis. There he walks slowly, head thrust forward, his eyes fixed on one point that seems a star to him, the corner of the Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire. The nearer he comes the more his eyes light up and the slower he goes, as though he fears the moment of arrival, like a magnetic needle trembling towards the pole. At last he reaches the corner, puts his head round the last house with melancholy timidity, gazes into the street with a look like the reflection of a closed paradise, and a single tear rolls down and sometimes stops at his mouth, where he tastes its bitterness. Then he goes back by the same road, his glance dying as he retreats.

Little by little he stops short of the corner: halfway along the Rue Saint-Louis, then at the Rue Culture-Sainte-Catherine, where he looks at the distant street and shakes his head as if refusing himself something; then the Rue Pavée, the Rue des Trois-Pavillons, finally no further than the Blancs-Manteaux. He is a pendulum no longer wound up, its swings shortening before they cease. Every day he leaves at the same hour on the same walk and never completes it, shortening it perhaps without knowing. His face says one thing: what is the use? His eye is dim and his tears are exhausted; his chin trembles; the folds of his gaunt neck are painful to see; in bad weather he carries an umbrella he never opens. The good women of the quarter say he is an innocent, and the children follow him and laugh.

title: Pity for the Unhappy, but Indulgence for the Happy
summary: Hugo explains, without condemning, why Marius has edged Jean Valjean out: he regrets his promise, has learned from a former Laffitte clerk something troubling about the money and refuses to touch it, and has set himself between Cosette and 'Monsieur Jean'; Cosette, wholly absorbed in her husband, lets herself forget, and is told he is away on a journey.
details: It is a terrible thing to be happy, Hugo begins: in possessing happiness one forgets duty. Yet the reader would be wrong to blame Marius. He put no questions to M. Fauchelevent before the marriage and has been afraid to put any to Jean Valjean since; he regrets the concession he made to despair, and has confined himself to gradually estranging Valjean from the house and effacing him from Cosette's mind, always placing himself between the two, so that the effacement became an eclipse. He believes he has serious reasons, some the reader has seen and others yet to be shown.

One of them is new: in a case he argued, Marius chanced to meet a former employee of the Laffitte bank and, without seeking it, acquired mysterious information which, out of respect for the secret he promised to keep and for Valjean's perilous position, he has not been able to probe. He believes he now has a grave duty, to restore the six hundred thousand francs to someone he is discreetly seeking; meanwhile he does not touch the money.

Cosette has been told none of these secrets, but it would be harsh to condemn her either. An all-powerful magnetism makes her do instinctively what Marius wishes; sensing his will towards 'Monsieur Jean', she conforms, and what is shadowed in his mind grows overcast in hers. Her forgetting is superficial, heedlessness rather than ingratitude; at bottom she is sincerely attached to the man she so long called father, but she loves her husband more. When she wonders aloud about him, Marius reminds her that he said he was going on a journey; two or three times she sends Nicolette to the Rue de l'Homme Armé, and Valjean has the answer 'no' returned. The couple themselves have been away, to Vernon, where Marius took Cosette to his father's grave. Marius gradually wins Cosette away from Jean Valjean, and Cosette allows it. Hugo closes on the 'ingratitude of nature': the young turn towards the light and the old towards the shadows, branches growing away from the trunk without breaking from it; let us not blame these poor children.

title: Last Flickerings of a Lamp Without Oil
summary: Jean Valjean sits one last time on the stone post where Gavroche found him, then takes to his bed and stops eating; his portress, the only soul he sees, scolds him, fetches the doctor of the quarter, and is told that the old man is dying of having lost someone dear to him, and that 'someone else' must come.
details: One day Jean Valjean goes down his staircase, takes three steps into the street, and sits on the stone post where Gavroche found him meditating on the night of the 5th to 6th of June; after a few moments he goes back up. It is the last swing of the pendulum. The next day he does not leave his apartment; the day after, he does not leave his bed. His portress, who cooks his scanty meals of cabbage or potatoes with bacon, finds the plate untouched; he protests that the water jug is empty, and she retorts that drinking without eating is called fever. He takes her hand and promises in his kind voice to eat the potatoes. He sees no other human being; he is in one of those Paris streets through which no one passes and houses to which no one comes. While he still went out he bought a little copper crucifix for a few sous and hung it opposite his bed.

A week passes and he has not taken a step in his room. The portress tells her husband the good man upstairs is not eating and will not last long; she is sure his daughter has made a bad marriage. The porter pronounces, with marital sovereignty, that if the man has a doctor he will die and if he has none he will die. Scraping grass from her pavement with an old knife, she grumbles that it is a shame, such a neat old man, white as a chicken. She spots the doctor of the quarter at the end of the street and sends him up; the door is always unlocked.

The doctor sees Jean Valjean and talks with him. Coming down, he tells the portress that her sick man is very ill indeed. What is wrong with him? 'Everything and nothing. He is a man who, to all appearances, has lost some person who is dear to him. People die of that.' He told the doctor he was in good health. The doctor will come again, 'but someone else besides must come.'

title: A Pen Is Heavy to the Man Who Lifted the Fauchelevent’s Cart
summary: Too weak to find his pulse, Jean Valjean dresses in his old workman's clothes, lays out Cosette's little mourning dress, lights candles in the Bishop's candlesticks in broad daylight, and begins a letter to Cosette explaining that the fortune is honestly hers, earned from his invention in the jet trade; he breaks off sobbing that he will die without seeing her, and there is a knock at the door.
details: One evening Jean Valjean can barely raise himself on his elbow, feels for his pulse and cannot find it, and knows he is weaker than he has ever been. Under some supreme preoccupation he forces himself up and dresses in the old workman's clothes he has returned to since he stopped going out, sweating and pausing at every movement. Since living alone he has moved his bed into the antechamber to inhabit the empty flat as little as possible. He opens the valise, spreads Cosette's little outfit on the bed, puts two wax candles into the Bishop's candlesticks on the chimneypiece and lights them, though it is still broad summer daylight, as candles are lit by day in rooms where there is a corpse.

He drops into the chair before the mirror in which he once read Cosette's reversed writing on the blotter, and does not recognise himself: he is eighty, and this one year has counted for thirty; the mark on his brow is not age but death. His sorrow has coagulated into a clot of despair. By night he drags a table and the armchair to the fireside, sets out pen, ink and paper, faints, tips the jug to his mouth because he cannot lift it, moistens the dried ink with water, and writes with the back of a curled pen, gazing for hours at the little black gown.

At last he writes: 'Cosette, I bless thee.' Her husband was right to make him understand he should go, though there is a little error in what he believed; he is excellent, and she must love him well after her father is dead. Then, so that she will know the money is really hers, he sets down the trade: white jet from Norway, black jet from England, black glass jewellery from Germany; the little anvil and spirit-lamp; the wax of resin and lampblack at four livres a pound that he learned to make from shellac and turpentine for thirty sous; buckles of violet glass fixed to black iron; Spain, the country of jet, buying a great deal. The pen falls from his fingers and he is seized by a sob from the depths of his being: all is over; she was a smile that passed over him; one minute, one instant, to hear her voice and touch her dress and then die; it is nothing to die, what is frightful is to die without seeing her. At that moment there is a knock at the door.

title: A Bottle of Ink Which Only Succeeded in Whitening
summary: A disguised Thénardier comes to sell Marius a secret about Jean Valjean and, trying to prove him a thief and murderer, instead proves with two old newspapers that Valjean was M. Madeleine and that Javert killed himself, then produces the strip of torn coat that shows it was Valjean who carried Marius through the sewer; Marius pays him to leave for America and rushes with Cosette to the Rue de l'Homme Armé.
details: That same evening Basque brings Marius a coarse letter whose tobacco smell and handwriting bring the Jondrette garret before him at once. Signed 'Thénard', it offers, for a consideration, to drive from his honourable family an individual who has no right there. Marius pockets some banknotes and has the man shown in: a stranger in green spectacles, plastered grey hair, a thick nose and a threadbare black suit too big for him, which Hugo identifies, in a digression on 'the Changer' of the Rue Beautreillis who rents respectable costumes to rogues at thirty sous a day, as the 'statesman, ex-ambassador' outfit. The visitor claims acquaintance with princesses and Chateaubriand, describes a fortified village called la Joya near Panama where gold is found, and says he needs money to emigrate there with his wife and daughter. He then offers, gratis, the news that Marius has a thief and assassin in his house named Jean Valjean, an ex-convict. 'I know it,' says Marius to each point, and when the man offers the secret of Madame la Baronne's fortune for twenty thousand francs, then ten, then twenty francs, Marius names him: Thénardier, also Jondrette, Fabantou, Genflot, Don Alvarès and Mistress Balizard, the innkeeper of Montfermeil. He throws him five hundred francs. Thénardier laughs, pulls off the spectacles and the quills from his nostrils, straightens his back and admits it. He has never seen Marius before; through Azelma's pursuit of the wedding party on Shrove Tuesday and his own inductions he has learned who the man in the sewer was and that the Baroness is Cosette, though he does not know exactly who Cosette is and thinks better of trading on Fantine's story.

Marius, glad at last to be able to pay his father's debt and to probe the origin of Cosette's fortune, tells Thénardier what he himself knows: Jean Valjean is a thief because he robbed and ruined a wealthy manufacturer, M. Madeleine of the Pas-de-Calais, extracting over half a million from Laffitte by a forged signature (Marius has this from the cashier himself), and an assassin because he shot the police agent Javert, as Marius saw at the barricade. 'Monsieur le Baron, we are on the wrong track,' says Thénardier, and gives two reasons: Jean Valjean did not rob M. Madeleine because Jean Valjean was M. Madeleine, and he did not kill Javert because Javert killed Javert. He produces two yellowed newspapers from a tobacco-soaked envelope: a Drapeau Blanc of the 25th of July 1823 establishing the identity of Madeleine and Valjean, and a Moniteur of the 15th of June 1832 announcing Javert's suicide and adding, from Javert's own report to the prefect, that he owed his life at the barricade to an insurgent who fired into the air instead of blowing out his brains. Marius cannot doubt printed proof; the cashier's information was false. He cries out with joy that the wretch is an admirable man, Madeleine, the providence of a whole countryside, Javert's saviour, a hero, a saint.

'He's not a saint,' says Thénardier, 'he's an assassin and a robber,' and he tells his real story. On the 6th of June 1832 a man who had made the Grand Sewer his hiding-place and held a key to it saw a bent figure approaching the outlet grating with a corpse on his back: an ex-convict who had crossed a frightful quagmire rather than leave the body where the sewermen would find it. The convict demanded the key; the other, parleying, tore a strip from the dead man's coat as evidence, let him out, and ran. The man with the corpse was Jean Valjean; the man with the key is Thénardier himself; and he holds up the strip of torn black cloth, stained dark. Marius, pale and breathless, fumbles in a cupboard without taking his eyes from the rag. As Thénardier concludes that the murdered young man was some rich stranger lured into a trap, Marius cries, 'The young man was myself, and here is the coat!', flings down his bloodstained coat, and fits the strip exactly to the tear.

Thénardier is petrified. Marius, trembling and radiant, thrusts a fistful of notes at him: he came to accuse the man and has justified him, he is himself the thief and the assassin, Marius saw him in the lair on the Rue de l'Hôpital and could send him to the galleys; here is a thousand francs; Waterloo protects him. ('Of a General,' Thénardier corrects, when Marius says he saved a colonel.) Marius adds three thousand more and promises twenty thousand on the day he leaves for America with his daughter, 'for your wife is dead, you abominable liar'. Hugo finishes with the man: two days later Thénardier sails under a false name with Azelma and a draft for twenty thousand francs on New York, and with Marius's money sets up in America as a slave-dealer. Marius rushes to the garden crying for Cosette, a carriage and her shawl: 'It was he who saved my life!' In the cab to No. 7 Rue de l'Homme Armé he pours it out: the letter sent by Gavroche must have reached him; he went to the barricade to save Marius, saved Javert too, carried him through the sewer and the quagmire to give him to Cosette; 'Thy father, Cosette, thy father more than ever'; they will bring him back whether he is willing or not. Cosette understands not a word and says, 'You are right.'

title: A Night Behind Which There Is Day
summary: Cosette and Marius burst in on the dying Jean Valjean, who asks their pardon and is asked for his; he tells them he is about to die, insists the fortune is honestly Cosette's, bequeaths her the candlesticks, asks for a nameless grave, tells Cosette her mother's name was Fantine, blesses them with his hands on their heads, and dies.
details: At the knock Valjean feebly says 'Come in', and Cosette rushes into the room while Marius stays leaning on the door-jamb. Valjean sits erect with trembling outstretched arms and an immense joy in his eyes; Cosette falls on his breast crying 'Father!' and he stammers, 'It is thou! Thou dost pardon me then!' Marius, holding back tears, murmurs 'My father!', and Valjean asks his pardon too and says, 'Thanks.' Cosette tosses off her shawl and hat, sits on his knees, parts his white hair and kisses his brow. He marvels at how stupid he was: at the very moment they were climbing the stairs he was telling himself he would never see her again; one reckons without the good God, who sends an angel to a good man who needs one. He admits he needed to see Cosette a little now and then, a heart needs a bone to gnaw, but he knew he was in the way. Cosette scolds him for his long 'journey' and his cold hands.

When Valjean again asks Marius's pardon, Marius bursts out to Cosette: this man saved his life and gave her to him and then sacrificed himself, and he, the ingrate, the pitiless one, is thanked by him; Cosette, that man is an angel. 'Hush, why tell all that?' Why, Marius demands, did he not say he was Monsieur Madeleine, that he saved Javert, that Marius owed him his life? Because, Valjean answers, he thought as Marius did, that he ought to go away; had Marius known about the sewer he would have made him stay. Marius declares they will carry him off, that he is Cosette's father and his, and he shall not pass another day in this dreadful house. 'Tomorrow I shall not be here, but I shall not be with you.' Cosette threatens to run away with him by force and chatters about his waiting chamber, the azaleas, her strawberries, the robin eaten by a cat, and the end of 'Madame' and 'Monsieur Jean' now that everyone says 'thou'. He hears the music of her voice rather than the words, murmurs that the proof God is good is that she is here, says how charming it would be to live together, and adds gently, 'It is a pity.' Then: 'I am going to die presently.' Cosette cries that she forbids it; he answers, 'Oh yes, forbid me to die. Who knows? Perhaps I shall obey'; Marius kneels and begs his forgiveness; Valjean says God has thought as they all have and does not change his mind, death is a good arrangement, and he drank the whole jug of water last night.

The doctor enters; Valjean greets him with 'Good day, and farewell', and the doctor answers Marius's one-word question with a glance and, feeling the pulse, whispers 'Too late'. 'It is nothing to die; it is dreadful not to live,' Valjean says. In a last access of strength he walks firmly to the wall, takes down the little copper crucifix and lays it on the table: 'Behold the great martyr.' Then he sinks, rallies, kisses a fold of Cosette's sleeve, and tells them what pained him most: that Marius would not touch the money. It is honestly Cosette's; he explains the jet and the iron slides for bracelets and refers them to the paper he was writing. When the portress asks whether he wants a priest he answers, 'I have had one,' pointing above his head; Hugo thinks it probable the Bishop was present at this death.

His breath failing, he calls them close for his last words: he loves them dearly, Cosette must weep for him a little but not too much, the buckles without tongues paid best of all so the six hundred thousand francs are honest money and she may have a carriage, a box at the theatre and fine dresses; she will find his letter; he leaves her the two candlesticks, silver but to him gold and diamonds, and does not know whether the one who gave them is pleased with him on high. He is to be buried in the first plot of earth they find, under a stone with no name on it. He asks Marius's pardon for not always having loved him; there is a five-hundred-franc note in the chest of drawers for the poor. He points to the little gown on the bed and remembers Montfermeil: the forest, the handle of the water-bucket, her cold red hand, the doll Catherine, the straws floated on the gutters, the battledore and shuttlecock, cherries in her ears. The Thénardiers were wicked and she must forgive them. 'Cosette, the moment has come to tell thee the name of thy mother. She was called Fantine. Kneel whenever thou utterest it. She suffered much. She loved thee dearly.' Love each other well and always, there is nothing else in the world. He confesses he went as far as the corner of the street like a madman, once without his hat. 'I die happy. Give me your dear and well-beloved heads, so that I may lay my hands upon them.' Cosette and Marius kneel under his hands, which no longer move. He has fallen back, lit by the candles, his white face turned to heaven. He is dead. The night is starless; no doubt some immense angel stands in the gloom with wings outspread, awaiting that soul.

title: The Grass Covers and the Rain Effaces
summary: In a deserted corner of Père-Lachaise, near the common grave, a plain nameless stone lies under a yew; four pencilled lines once written on it, saying that he sleeps, that he lived despite a strange fate and died when he lost his angel, as simply as night comes when day departs, have long since been effaced by rain and dust.
details: In the cemetery of Père-Lachaise, near the common grave and far from the fashionable tombs, in a deserted corner by an old wall, under a great yew climbed by wild convolvulus, among dandelions and moss, lies a stone. Time, damp and lichen have worked on it as on any other; the water greens it and the air blackens it. It is near no path, the grass is high and wet, lizards come when there is sun, weeds quiver all around, and in spring linnets sing in the trees.

The stone is perfectly plain, cut only to be long enough and narrow enough to cover a man. No name is to be read on it. Only, many years ago, a hand pencilled four lines of French verse upon it, which rain and dust have gradually made illegible and which are probably effaced today. They say that he sleeps; that though fate was strange to him, he lived; that he died when he no longer had his angel; and that the thing came about simply of itself, as night falls when the day departs.
